newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes rules on access to telecoms networks.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes rules on access to telecoms networks.

text.p: The European Commission proposed rules on Tuesday to enable new telecommunication companies to compete fairly with the current monopoly operators from 1998 when the European telecoms market is to be fully liberalised.

In a draft notice due to be published shortly for public consultation, the Commission stressed that new service providers must be allowed to hook up to the networks of existing operators at fair terms.
Otherwise, it said, the Commission could fine them for abusing a dominant position.

Even after the telecoms sector is thrown open to competition on January 1, 1998, newcomers will have to rely largely on the infrastructure owned by long-established national operators such as France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom.

"Three important elements relating to access which could be manipulated by the access provider, in effect, to refuse to provide access are timing, technical configuration and price," says the notice, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

The Commission does not say how quickly phone companies must respond to a request for access, nor what price they should charge. But it left no doubt that "undue and unexplained delays" -- which it would measure against the normal practice in the market -- constitute an abuse.
The Commission also described "excessively high prices" and "unfairly low prices" as examples of abuses.
"Excessive pricing for access as well as being abusive in itself, may also amount to an effective refusal to grant access," the text said.
The situation of unfairly low prices could arise if a dominant network operator charged a price below cost to eliminate competition from other, emerging infrastructure providers.

Under EU legislation that came into force last July, utility companies such as railways must be allowed to use their own so-called alternative infrastructure to provide telecoms services. But the Commission acknowledges that it may take some time before this becomes reality.

The Commission also said it would take action against any restrictions on competition stemming from access agreements themselves -- for example, exclusivity obligations aimed at keeping other competitors at bay or clauses designed to coordinate prices or share markets.

The risk of price coordination was particularly high in the telecoms sector since "interconnection charges often amount to 50 percent or more of the total cost of the services provided", the notice said.
The Commission, which has the power to adopt the notice without approval of EU governments, said it would finalise the text after receiving comments from interested parties.
